info.bio: The Germs son una banda estadounidense de punk rock procedente de Los Ángeles, California, originalmente activo desde 1977 hasta 1980 (Posteriormente reunido en el 2005). La primera alineación del grupo estaba compuesta por el cantante Darby Crash, el guitarrista Pat Smear, la bajista Lorna Doom y el baterista Don Bolles. Sólamente lograron editar un álbum (GI) en 1979, producido por Joan Jett, un año después de disolvió por el suicidio de Crash.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk como «violento, rápido y ruidoso» tarda en conquistar EE UU, pero cuando lo hace el hardcore se convierte durante dos décadas en el idioma nacional de millones de chavales. Misfits y el «scum-rock»; el crossover punk-metal (Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion Of Conformity, Agnostic Front); Mission Of Burma en Boston. Washington: Bad Brains (reggae, funk y metal diez años por delante), Minor Threat (el «straight-edge») y Rites Of Spring, inventores del emo-core. San Francisco: Dead Kennedys de Jello Biafra, D.R.I. (thrash antes que Metallica), Flipper. Los «beach punks» de Los Ángeles: Germs, X, Black Flag (Damaged), Descendents, Gun Club (Fire Of Love), Bad Religion. El jazz-core de Minutemen y Saccharine Trust; en el Medio Oeste, Husker Du y Replacements cambian el hardcore para siempre; en Chicago, Naked Raygun y Big Black de Steve Albini; en Europa, The Ex y los italianos CCCP.

podcast.title: Darby Crash's Death
podcast.body: The band's leader, Darby Crash, tragically took his own life on December 7, 1980, via a heroin overdose in a suicide pact with a friend. This event occurred the day before John Lennon was shot, and notably, his friend survived the pact. "Crash took his own life by OD on heroin in a suicide pact with a friend on December 7, 1980, the day before John Lennon was shot."

podcast.title: Darby Crash's Untimely Death
podcast.body: Darby Crash died of a heroin overdose on December 7, 1980, tragically just one day before the assassination of John Lennon. This unfortunate timing meant his death was largely overshadowed and almost lost to history. "He was almost lost to history because he had the misfortune of dying of a heroin overdose one day before John Lennon was assassinated."

podcast.title: Early Sound Comparison
podcast.body: The Germs' first proper show recording, titled "Germicide" from the summer of 1977, was perceived by guitarist Pat Smear as sounding like Alice Cooper, despite being a burgeoning punk rock act. This highlights their initial sonic aspirations before fully embracing the punk identity. "If you ever listen to the first germs recording, which is our first proper show, which is the thing, who called germicide, we think we sound like Alaskupper."

podcast.title: Influence of The Ramones
podcast.body: The Germs were among hundreds of bands that emerged following the Ramones' continuous touring, drawing inspiration from their raw and straightforward punk approach. "The germs were one of literally hundreds of bands that spring up in the wake of the Ramones, who were on the road almost continuously."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for Bad Religion
podcast.body: The Germs were cited as an inspiration for the high school students who formed Bad Religion in 1980, encouraging them to be part of the hardcore movement. "They came together in 1980, when a bunch of high school students, inspired by the likes of Black Flag, the Circle Jerks, and the germs, decided that they wanted a piece of the reaction."

podcast.title: Pat Smear's Pre-Nirvana Band
podcast.body: Before joining Nirvana as a touring guitarist, Pat Smear was a member of The Germs. The band's singer, Darby Crash, died of a heroin overdose in 1980, marking one of Smear's early experiences with bandmate loss. "And before that, he was in the germs."

podcast.title: Simple, Fast Punk Ethos
podcast.body: Like the Ramones and English punk bands, The Germs demonstrated that impactful music could be made by playing just two chords very fast for approximately two minutes, emphasizing simplicity and raw energy. "Like them in the English punks, the germs showed everyone that you could play two chords very fast for two minutes, and that was really all you needed to do."

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: Pat Smear's early listening habits, before punk rock, included progressive and mainstream rock artists like Yes, Queen, Alice Cooper, and David Bowie, alongside The Runaways. He later embraced punk rock when the scene became open to bands like The Germs who "didn't know how to play." "I was listening to yes. I was listening to Queen and a Alaskupper and David Bowie."

xref.body: Pat Smear recalls that when The Germs recorded their first proper show, known as "Germicide," in the summer of 1977, the band genuinely believed they sounded like Alice Cooper, despite their raw, emerging punk sound.
